goal:
SMART Goal 1 — Causes
By the end of this module, I will be able to identify and explain the primary
natural and anthropogenic drivers of climate change, including the greenhouse
effect, CO2 and methane emissions, deforestation, and ocean heat absorption,
well enough to explain each cause to a peer without referencing notes.

SMART Goal 2 — Feedback Loops
By the end of this module, I will be able to describe at least four major
climate feedback mechanisms (ice-albedo, water vapor, permafrost methane,
cloud feedbacks), correctly classifying each as positive or negative feedback,
and draw a labeled feedback loop diagram for at least two of them from memory.

SMART Goal 3 — Tipping Points & Systems Thinking
By the end of this module, I will be able to define climate tipping points,
name at least three examples (e.g., Amazon dieback, West Antarctic Ice Sheet,
Atlantic circulation collapse), and explain how crossing a tipping point can
trigger cascading effects across interconnected Earth systems.

SMART Goal 4 — Global Policy Responses
By the end of this module, I will be able to compare and contrast the major
international climate policy frameworks — the Kyoto Protocol, the Paris
Agreement, and the COP process — evaluating their mechanisms, commitments,
and limitations, and articulate at least two market-based instruments (carbon
tax, cap-and-trade) in plain language.

SMART Goal 5 — Mitigation vs. Adaptation
By the end of this module, I will be able to distinguish mitigation strategies
(reducing emissions: renewables, electrification, carbon capture) from
adaptation strategies (responding to impact: flood defenses, drought-resistant
crops, managed retreat) and apply this distinction to evaluate a real-world
national policy example.

Prior Knowledge: General high school science background; familiar with basic
chemistry (greenhouse gases) but not with feedback systems or policy
frameworks at any depth.

Motivation: I want to engage confidently in climate policy debates, understand
news reporting on climate negotiations (e.g., COP summits), and apply
systems-thinking skills to other complex global problems.
notes_from_mentor:
The student came in with strong motivation around real-world relevance —
specifically wanting to understand climate news coverage and policy debates —
but with limited background beyond high school science. The main gaps
identified were: (1) no prior exposure to systems thinking or feedback loop
diagrams, (2) confusion between weather and climate at the mechanistic level,
and (3) no awareness of how international policy instruments actually work
(e.g., the difference between a carbon tax and cap-and-trade).

MENTOR GUIDANCE FOR CONTENT GENERATION:

1. Sequencing: Start with a clear conceptual anchor — the difference between
   weather and climate — before introducing the greenhouse effect. Many
   students conflate the two, which undermines everything downstream.
   Establish this distinction on the very first slide or section.

2. Feedback Loops: This is the conceptually hardest section. The student
   finds abstract systems notation confusing. Favor concrete, real-world
   examples first (e.g., melting Arctic ice exposing darker ocean surface),
   then introduce the diagram. Use the ice-albedo feedback as the teaching
   example because it is the most visually intuitive. Avoid introducing more
   than two feedback loops per slide.

3. Tipping Points: Frame tipping points using a physical analogy first —
   e.g., a ball balanced on a hill — before applying it to climate. This
   scaffolds the abstraction. Include a world map showing approximate
   locations of major tipping elements; the spatial dimension significantly
   aids retention here.

4. Policy Section: The student has no economics background. Avoid jargon-
   heavy finance language. Explain carbon pricing with a simple supply-
   demand intuition before comparing Kyoto vs. Paris. A comparison table
   (Kyoto vs. Paris: scope, enforcement, temperature targets, participation)
   is strongly recommended. Highlight the NDC (Nationally Determined
   Contributions) mechanism as the key structural innovation of Paris.

5. Mitigation vs. Adaptation: Treat this as the synthesis section. The
   student specifically asked to understand "what countries are actually
   doing." Use real country examples — Germany (Energiewende), Bangladesh
   (adaptation planning), Netherlands (coastal management) — to make policy
   concrete. Avoid generic lists; anchor every strategy to a real case.

6. Tone and Register: The student engages well with narrative framing.
   Where possible, open each section with a question or a striking data
   point (e.g., "2023 was the hottest year in 125,000 years of recorded
   proxy data") rather than a definition. This keeps the lesson from feeling
   like a textbook.

7. Visual Priority: This topic is inherently visual. Every section should
   include at least one diagram or data visualization. Recommended visuals:
   - Keeling Curve (atmospheric CO2 since 1958)
   - Diagram of the greenhouse effect with labeled energy flows
   - Feedback loop diagrams (ice-albedo, water vapor)
   - Map of climate tipping elements
   - Temperature anomaly graph (IPCC AR6 baseline)
   - Comparison infographic: mitigation vs. adaptation strategies

KEY LEARNING OUTCOME (for course outline generation):
   By the end of this module, the student should be able to explain why the
   climate system responds non-linearly to emissions, describe the main
   feedback mechanisms that amplify warming, and critically evaluate the
   architecture and limitations of the Paris Agreement — well enough to
   participate in an informed discussion of climate policy.

outline.summary: This 19-lesson module builds a comprehensive understanding of climate science and policy by carefully managing cognitive load. It scaffolds foundational mechanisms (weather vs. climate, greenhouse effect) before introducing complex, non-linear systems like feedback loops and tipping points. Using narrative hooks, visual aids, and concrete analogies, the curriculum then bridges science and economics to demystify carbon pricing, international frameworks (Paris Agreement, COP), and real-world national strategies for mitigation and adaptation.

lessons.title: 1.1 Weather vs. Climate: The Fundamental Difference
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'If it snowed today, does that mean global warming is fake?' Begin with the critical distinction between weather (short-term local conditions) and climate (long-term statistical averages). Use concrete analogies, like weather being your mood and climate being your personality, to prevent downstream conflation of these concepts. Introduce the baseline reality: 2023 was the hottest year in over 125,000 years of proxy data.
lessons.objective: Distinguish between weather and climate at a mechanistic level to accurately interpret short-term meteorological events versus long-term global trends.

lessons.title: 1.2 The Greenhouse Effect and Earth's Energy Flow
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'Why isn't Earth a frozen ball of ice?' Introduce the natural greenhouse effect. Visual required: A labeled diagram of the greenhouse effect showing incoming solar radiation and outgoing infrared radiation trapped by greenhouse gases. Explain the basic chemistry of CO2 and methane, emphasizing how they interact with heat.
lessons.objective: Explain the mechanics of the greenhouse effect and trace the flow of energy into and out of the Earth's atmosphere.

lessons.title: 1.3 Natural vs. Anthropogenic Drivers
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'How do we know it is us?' Visual required: The Keeling Curve showing atmospheric CO2 since 1958. Differentiate between natural climate cycles (orbital variations, volcanoes) and anthropogenic drivers (fossil fuels, deforestation). Introduce the role of oceans in absorbing excess heat, explaining why surface temperatures don't tell the whole story.
lessons.objective: Identify and explain the primary natural and anthropogenic drivers of climate change, specifically detailing human-caused CO2, methane emissions, and ocean heat absorption.

lessons.title: 2.1 Introduction to Systems: Positive vs. Negative Feedbacks
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'What happens when warming causes even more warming?' Introduce systems thinking without abstract math. Define feedback loops: positive (amplifying) and negative (balancing). Provide a simple real-world analogy outside of climate science, like a microphone screeching next to a speaker, to ground the concept before applying it to Earth.
lessons.objective: Define positive and negative feedback loops and explain how they act as amplifiers or balancers within a system.

lessons.title: 2.2 The Ice-Albedo Feedback Loop
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'Why is the Arctic warming four times faster than the rest of the planet?' Visual required: Ice-albedo feedback loop diagram. Walk through the physical process: melting white ice exposes dark ocean, which absorbs more heat, melting more ice. This is the primary visual and intuitive anchor for teaching positive climate feedbacks.
lessons.objective: Describe and draw a labeled feedback loop diagram for the ice-albedo effect from memory.

lessons.title: 2.3 Water Vapor and Cloud Feedbacks
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'Can water act as a greenhouse gas?' Explore how a warmer atmosphere holds more water vapor, amplifying the greenhouse effect (positive feedback). Then, introduce cloud feedbacks, explaining the complex dual role clouds play (reflecting sunlight vs. trapping heat). Limit to these two feedbacks to manage cognitive load.
lessons.objective: Explain the mechanisms of water vapor and cloud feedbacks, classifying their roles as positive or negative amplifiers of global warming.

lessons.title: 2.4 The Permafrost Methane Feedback
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'What is sleeping beneath the Siberian ice?' Explore the thawing of permafrost and the release of trapped methane. Compare the warming potential of methane to CO2. Visual required: Diagram showing the cyclical nature of thawing permafrost leading to gas release and further atmospheric warming.
lessons.objective: Diagram the permafrost methane feedback loop from memory and explain why methane release represents a critical positive feedback.

lessons.title: 3.1 Understanding Tipping Points: The Ball on a Hill Analogy
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'When does a pushed glass fall off the table?' Introduce the concept of non-linear responses and tipping points. Scaffold the abstraction using the physical analogy of a ball balanced on the crest of a hill—once pushed over the edge, the system enters a new state and cannot easily be pushed back, even if the initial force is removed.
lessons.objective: Define climate tipping points using physical analogies to explain non-linear system responses.

lessons.title: 3.2 Mapping Global Tipping Elements
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'Where are the Earth's Achilles heels?' Visual required: A world map showing approximate locations of major tipping elements. Focus on three critical examples: Amazon rainforest dieback, West Antarctic Ice Sheet collapse, and the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) slowdown. Spatial visualization is key for retention here.
lessons.objective: Name and locate at least three major global climate tipping points and describe the physical changes associated with each.

lessons.title: 3.3 Cascading Effects and Systemic Risk
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'How does melting ice in Greenland cause drought in South America?' Connect the tipping points discussed in the previous lesson. Explain how crossing one tipping point can trigger a domino effect across interconnected Earth systems. Emphasize that climate systems do not operate in isolated silos.
lessons.objective: Explain how crossing a single climate tipping point can trigger cascading, domino-like effects across other interconnected global Earth systems.

lessons.title: 4.1 The Economics of Emissions: Intro to Carbon Pricing
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'Why is it free to pollute the atmosphere?' Introduce the basic economics of climate change using simple supply and demand intuition, completely avoiding finance jargon. Explain the concept of 'externalities' and why economists argue that putting a price on carbon is the most efficient way to reduce emissions.
lessons.objective: Explain the fundamental economic rationale for pricing carbon emissions using basic supply and demand intuition.

lessons.title: 4.2 Market Instruments: Carbon Tax vs. Cap-and-Trade
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'Should we tax pollution or trade the right to pollute?' Clearly define and contrast the two primary market-based instruments. Explain a Carbon Tax (fixed price, variable emissions reduction) versus Cap-and-Trade (fixed emissions limit, variable price). Use simple, plain-language examples for each.
lessons.objective: Compare and contrast a carbon tax and a cap-and-trade system, articulating the mechanics of each in plain language.

lessons.title: 4.3 International Frameworks: The Kyoto Protocol
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'Why did our first global attempt to stop climate change fail?' Visual required: Temperature anomaly graph with IPCC AR6 baseline. Review the history and mechanics of the Kyoto Protocol. Discuss its top-down structure, the division between developed and developing nations, and its ultimate limitations in enforcing global targets.
lessons.objective: Evaluate the Kyoto Protocol, identifying its core mechanisms and the structural limitations that hindered its success.

lessons.title: 4.4 The Paris Agreement and NDCs
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'How did the world finally agree on climate action in 2015?' Visual required: Comparison table of Kyoto vs. Paris (scope, enforcement, temperature targets, participation). Highlight the structural innovation of the Paris Agreement: bottom-up, Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). Explain how the 'ratchet mechanism' is supposed to increase ambition over time.
lessons.objective: Analyze the architecture of the Paris Agreement, distinguishing it from Kyoto, and explain the function of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs).

lessons.title: 4.5 The COP Process: How Climate Negotiations Work
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'What actually happens when 70,000 people fly to a climate summit?' Demystify the annual Conference of the Parties (COP). Explain the negotiation process, how consensus is reached, the role of non-state actors, and how to critically read news coverage of COP outcomes and pledges.
lessons.objective: Describe the annual COP negotiation process and critically evaluate the achievements and shortcomings of these global summits.

lessons.title: 5.1 Defining the Divide: Mitigation vs. Adaptation
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'Do we focus on preventing the fire, or fireproofing the house?' Visual required: Comparison infographic outlining Mitigation vs. Adaptation. Define Mitigation (reducing the causes: renewables, electrification, carbon capture) and Adaptation (managing the impacts: flood defenses, managed retreat, drought-resistant crops).
lessons.objective: Distinguish between mitigation and adaptation strategies, accurately categorizing examples of climate interventions into the correct group.

lessons.title: 5.2 Mitigation in Action: Germany's Energiewende
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'How does an industrial powerhouse quit fossil fuels?' Dive into a concrete, real-world mitigation case study. Explore Germany's 'Energiewende' (energy transition) policy. Look at their shift to renewables, the challenges of grid infrastructure, and the geopolitical realities of electrification.
lessons.objective: Analyze a real-world national mitigation strategy, identifying the technological shifts and structural challenges involved in reducing emissions.

lessons.title: 5.3 Adaptation in Action: Bangladesh and the Netherlands
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'How do you survive when your country is sinking?' Explore two contrasting adaptation case studies. Look at the Netherlands' high-tech coastal management (Delta Works, Room for the River) and Bangladesh's community-level adaptation planning (early warning systems, floating agriculture). Anchor the strategies to the realities of different economic resources.
lessons.objective: Evaluate national adaptation strategies by comparing high-infrastructure approaches with community-resilience planning in vulnerable regions.

lessons.title: 5.4 Synthesis: Evaluating Comprehensive Climate Policy
lessons.main_content: Hook: 'What does a perfect climate plan look like?' A synthesis lesson combining systems thinking, policy frameworks, and mitigation/adaptation. Have the student review a real or simulated national climate pledge (NDC) and evaluate it based on its grasp of feedback risks, carbon pricing mechanisms, and balance of adaptation vs. mitigation.
lessons.objective: Synthesize knowledge of climate feedbacks, economics, and international frameworks to critically evaluate a comprehensive national climate policy.

courseName: Eval 9: Climate Change — Causes, Feedback Loops & Global Policy Responses
